Tanvir, you keep saying you want to earn something on the side. Let your Jahnavi Bua tell you how I started, back in my second year of college.
I didn't begin with ideas. I sat on the hostel floor with a notebook and drew two columns. Left side: what can I actually do? Maths tutoring, neat handwriting, fast typing. Right side: where are my free hours? I went day by day. Classes till four, lab on Tuesday and Thursday, the long bus ride home every Saturday.
When I added it up, I had maybe eight free hours a week, not the twenty I'd imagined. So I crossed out the typing job that wanted afternoons, and kept tutoring two children in my own building on weekday evenings. It fit, and I never once had to cancel on them.
That's all I'm telling you, Tanvir. Count first, then choose.

The coaching centre wanted an answer by nine that night, and the hostel lights had gone out at seven. Payal sat on the stairwell with her phone torch and a torn page, Deepak beside her swatting mosquitoes.
'Just say yes,' he said. 'They pay per class.'

'They want four evenings.'
'Then I can't give them four evenings.'
At eight-forty she messaged the centre: three evenings, chemistry only. The reply came quickly: start with two, and we'll see. Payal wrote the new number under her list and felt her shoulders drop.

I've now asked the family to move two sessions a week online, and I'm working out what hourly rate would feel fair.

Anirban edited wedding videos for a small studio run by Lakshmi, and the work never ran out. In his first month he worked whenever files arrived, sometimes till 2 a.m., and slept through two morning lectures.
So he set it down in steps. First, he blocked Monday to Friday, 7 to 9 p.m., on the calendar pinned above his desk: ten hours a week, no more. Second, he marked his three weeks of semester exams in red, with no editing at all. Third, he told Lakshmi the plan before the wedding season began.
The test came in November. Lakshmi's biggest client wanted a video early, in the very week of his first exam. She called on a Tuesday. 'Just this once, the weekend?'
Anirban looked at the red week. 'Not this week. I can start Monday, 7 p.m.'
Lakshmi sighed, but moved the client's date. By December his lab reports were on time again.

In early September Varun told me he was doing three things at once: tutoring two Class 10 students, freelance slide design, and online data entry for a small firm. He wasn't sure which was worth it. I suggested he log hours and payments for a month.

Friday, 9 p.m. (Preeti's diary)
Got ₹3,600 from the Class 8 tuition today. Before I could even think about the jacket in the Sarojini lane, I did what Vandana Masi told me to try in April: ₹1,200 straight into the steel box marked 'fees + emergencies', the rest in my wallet.
Four months of this now. The box has ₹3,700, even after paying my exam form fee last month without asking Papa. That felt good in a quiet way.
The first weeks were annoying. I'd look at the box and think of momos. Now I don't open it unless it's real.
Today Isha from class borrowed my notes and said she was broke again, three days after her payment came in. I didn't lecture her. I just remembered being exactly that.
Jacket next month, maybe. From the other two-thirds.

qa.q: How much went into the steel box today?
qa.a: ₹1,200 straight into the steel box.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel about the box now compared with the first weeks?
qa.a: At first it felt annoying and tempting, but now there is a quiet pride and calm in having money ready for real needs.

qa.q: What else could help Preeti keep the box working when the jacket tempts again?
qa.a: Deciding in advance what counts as 'real' for opening it, and talking to Vandana Masi if a big need comes up.

qa.q: How might Vandana Masi see the last four months?
qa.a: Vandana Masi would likely be pleased that the April idea became a habit, one that paid the exam form fee without anyone asking Papa.

grounding: Shows a student setting aside a third of every payment for fees and emergencies so earnings become steady support.
